paper.abstract: Abstract Constraint pruning saves queries to a large language model (LLM) or another noisy oracle by skipping each yes/no question implied by answers accepted earlier, for example through transitivity. Entity-resolution systems and LLM-based rankers use this idea. However, their analyses typically assume a correct oracle. We argue that pruning should be judged by its risk when the oracle errs, since an accepted wrong answer spreads to every question it implies. When each answer is wrong independently with small probability ε \varepsilon , the first-order risk is set by how many facts one wrong answer corrupts on average. We consider two kinds of constraints. For implication rules, as in taxonomies, pruning in a random order adds no first-order risk: a wrong answer that would change k k facts is accepted with probability 1 / k 1/k , so it costs one fact on average. Rules with s s premises break this balance: a wrong answer at a premise shared by r r rules can cost order r 1 − 1 / s r^{1-1/s} facts. For entity resolution with m m records of one entity, the first-order risk equals ε \varepsilon times the Wiener index (the total pairwise distance) of the spanning tree built by the query order. Pivot orders, which first compare one record with all others, amplify errors by less than 2 and are optimal; random orders by order m 1 / 3 m^{1/3} ; the common most-similar-first order is the worst in one dimension and, for large m m , worse than random in two. With several entities, the cost of wrongly merging two does not depend on how many others exist. Simulations agree with every predicted constant within sampling error.

sections.heading: 1 INTRODUCTION
sections.text: Constraint pruning reduces the cost of collecting related yes/no facts from an oracle, such as an LLM or a human annotator, whose answers may be wrong. In entity resolution, a system asks whether two records refer to the same entity and skips pairs implied by transitivity ( Wang et al., 2013 ; Vesdapunt et al., 2014 ) . For example, accepting that A A and B B are the same and that B B and C C are the same determines the answer for A A and C C without another query. Similar propagation occurs when enforcing entailment and contradiction constraints between LLM beliefs ( Mitchell et al., 2022 ) , skipping comparisons in LLM ranking ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ) , or propagating orientation hints in causal discovery ( Meek, 1995 ; Long et al., 2023 ; Lyu et al., 2026 ) . However, an accepted error can also propagate to unqueried facts. If A A , B B and C C belong to one entity, a correct “same” answer for A , B A,B followed by a wrong “different” answer for B , C B,C implies a wrong “different” answer for A , C A,C . In the synthetic citation records of Figure 1 , one oracle error thus produces two final wrong decisions and saves one query, and the output is still logically consistent. Query counts alone cannot capture this cost. Prior work studies recovery probabilities, assumes deterministic oracles or examines the robustness of query structures ( Long et al., 2023 ; Hiremath et al., 2026 ; Agrawal et al., 2026 ; Galhotra et al., 2018 ) . Figure 1: Propagation in three synthetic citation records of one publication: one wrong answer produces two wrong pair decisions and saves one query. We study greedy closure decoding : process questions in an order, skip those implied by accepted answers, and otherwise query and accept the oracle’s answer, without revisiting earlier decisions. We measure risk by the expected number of final wrong facts, including inferred ones. The raw baseline asks every question and uses its answer unchanged, without enforcing consistency. Both procedures use the same potential answers: the answers the oracle would give if each question were asked. In single-error analysis , we make one potential answer wrong and keep all others correct. We count the final wrong facts caused by each error location, averaging over query orders when they are random. In Figure 1 , damage is 2; it is 0 if earlier correct answers imply and skip the wrong question. Under independent errors of small probability ε \varepsilon ( Long et al., 2023 ; Hiremath et al., 2026 ) , events with two or more errors have probability O ⁡ ( ε 2 ) O(\varepsilon^{2}) for a fixed finite instance. A reduction lemma expresses risk as ε \varepsilon times the sum of single-error damages, plus O ⁡ ( ε 2 ) O(\varepsilon^{2}) . The term linear in ε \varepsilon is the first-order risk ; its ratio to the raw baseline’s n ​ ε n\varepsilon is the error amplification , where n n counts questions. Random-order ranking and Meek propagation are not analyzed. Using single-error analysis, we derive the following first-order risk laws: • Risk conservation for pairwise constraints. For every satisfiable 2-CNF theory, including implications and pairwise contradictions, uniformly random orders give mean single-error damage 1 for unfixed facts and 0 for facts fixed by the constraints. Pruning therefore does not increase first-order risk over raw decoding ( Section 4 ). • Error amplification through a shared premise. For k k Horn rules with s ≥ 2 s\geq 2 premises each and one shared false premise, we derive the exact mean damage of a single wrong answer there, growing as Θ ⁡ ( k 1 − 1 / s ) \Theta(k^{1-1/s}) under uniformly random orders, for fixed s s ( Theorem 6 ). • Relating query order to tree structure. For m m records of one entity, independent errors at a common rate give first-order risk equal to that rate times the noiseless query tree’s Wiener index (total pairwise tree distance). Pivot stars minimize this risk among greedy orders, with amplification below 2; random orders give Θ ⁡ ( m 1 / 3 ) \Theta(m^{1/3}) , and similarity-first can be worse under Theorem 11 ’s embedding assumptions. We also give bounds for multiple errors at any error rate ( Section 5.1 ). • Locality of a single false merge. With only one wrong answer, false-merge damage depends only on the two affected entities. This yields separate within-entity and cross-entity first-order risks. We give bounds, exact small cases and the pivot pipeline’s exact first-order formula; the large-cluster growth exponent remains a conjecture ( Section 5.2 ). We test the theoretical predictions and compare query orders using simulations and LLM answers on the Cora citation data ( Section 6 ).

sections.heading: Noisy recovery and tree structure.
sections.text: Work on probabilistic unclean databases relates integrity constraints to minimum-repair and maximum-likelihood decoding ( De Sa et al., 2019 ; Gilad et al., 2023 ) . Other studies consider noisy graph-label recovery ( Globerson et al., 2015 ; Foster et al., 2018 ; Heidari et al., 2020 ; Lee et al., 2022 ; Jin et al., 2026 ) , correlation clustering ( Makarychev et al., 2015 ) , same-cluster queries ( Mazumdar and Saha, 2017b ) and noisy sorting ( Feige et al., 1994 ; Braverman and Mossel, 2008 ) . Their main goals are query efficiency or global recovery guarantees, usually at constant noise ( Banerjee and Shen, 2022 ) . Our tree-based analysis uses Kruskal’s construction ( Kruskal, 1956 ) , extremal properties of the Wiener index ( Dobrynin et al., 2001 ) , and results on random and spatial spanning trees ( Addario-Berry et al., 2009 ; Addario-Berry et al., 2017 ; Aizenman et al., 1999 ) .

sections.heading: Entity resolution and LLM comparisons.
sections.text: Crowdsourced entity resolution uses transitivity ( Wang et al., 2013 ; Vesdapunt et al., 2014 ) . Analyses of query ordering typically assume a correct oracle ( Firmani et al., 2016 ; Mazumdar and Saha, 2017a ) ; robust methods add verification queries ( Galhotra et al., 2018 ) or weaken transitivity ( Gruenheid et al., 2015 ) . Recent LLM work studies prompt sensitivity ( Gui et al., 2026 ) and matching errors ( Peeters et al., 2025 ) , compares matching strategies ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , filters candidates using matching feedback ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , and balances quality and cost through operator and model selection ( Guo et al., 2026 ) . Ranking work addresses non-transitive preferences and baseline-sensitive rankings ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , presentation-order and transitivity inconsistencies ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) , and risks from long inference chains ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ) . These studies improve matching, ranking or query allocation. We analyze how an accepted wrong answer causes errors in inferred decisions.

sections.heading: Logical consistency and causal hints.
sections.text: Belief-correction methods enforce entailment and contradiction relations ( Mitchell et al., 2022 ) . Logic.py translates natural-language puzzles into formal problems for a constraint solver ( Kesseli et al., 2025 ) . Causal discovery methods elicit and propagate hints about edge orientations ( Long et al., 2023 ; Lyu et al., 2026 ; Kıcıman et al., 2024 ) , while Guess2Graph uses unreliable expert guesses to order conditional-independence tests ( Hiremath et al., 2026 ) . These methods correct answers or select hints. We study a sequential decoding process that accepts oracle answers in order and keeps accepted answers fixed during subsequent inference.

sections.heading: 5 ENTITY RESOLUTION WITH TRANSITIVITY PRUNING
sections.text: We now apply the greedy-decoding framework to entity resolution, where each pairwise answer states whether two records refer to the same entity. Transitivity lets “same” on A A – B B and B B – C C imply “same” on A A – C C , saving a query but potentially spreading an error. This involves three pairwise facts, so the 2-CNF conservation law in Section 4 does not directly apply. We first study false splits within one entity, then false merges between entities.

sections.heading: Real LLM answers.
sections.text: In Cora ( Hasso Plattner Institute, n.d. ) , each entity comprises citation records of one paper. We use 62,423 within-entity pairs from 23 entities with at least 20 records. Qwen2.5-1.5B (base) ( Qwen Team, 2024 ) answers 6.6% wrongly. All orders reuse cached answers; similarity-first follows decreasing textual similarity. Pivot loses less than random order, while similarity-first has the lowest point estimate ( Table 3 ). Pooled answer-error rates on noiseless query-tree edges are 2.2% for similarity-first, 8.4% for pivot and 8.6% for random order, linking loss to both tree shape and edge accuracy. Pivot beats random order at all tested thresholds (approximately 1%–20% answer-error rates; Table 8 ). Redistributing each entity’s errors uniformly, with error counts fixed and query orders matched, raises all three losses and removes similarity-first’s advantage over pivot ( Table 3 , rows 2–3). Thus error locations matter. In six blocks of three or four similar entities, both false merges and false splits can occur; pivot has the lowest pooled loss. Appendix C gives the prompting protocol, threshold sweep and detailed results for these settings.

sections.heading: 7 DISCUSSION
sections.text: We analyzed error propagation in greedy, constraint-based decoding. Under uniformly random query orders, 2-CNF constraints do not increase first-order risk over raw answers, while shared-premise Horn rules can amplify errors. In record matching, one-entity first-order risk is determined by pairwise distances on the noiseless query tree. Under independent, equal-rate errors, pivot minimizes this risk among greedy orders. With one wrong answer, false merges affect only two entities. Simulations support the formulas and show pivot’s advantage over random order at the tested higher error rates. The Cora results show that tree shape and error locations both matter: uniformly redistributing errors removes similarity-first’s advantage over pivot. Future work could study interacting errors, especially false merges, across more models and datasets. The general Horn false-positive damage bound and false-merge growth law remain conjectures.

sections.text:
We first express small-noise risk in terms of single-error damage, then prove the results for logical constraints, entity resolution and sorting. Numerical checks are in Section B . sections.text: There are n n keys, which we identify with their true ranks 1 , … , n 1,\dots,n . The order code has one coordinate for each of the ( n 2 ) \binom{n}{2} pairs of keys, and its codewords are the n ! n! total orders. The answer on a pair is its orientation, that is, which of the two keys is smaller. Each answer is wrong with probability p p , independently over the pairs. The loss is the number of pairs that the output order inverts; this is the Hamming distance on the order code. The raw decoder has risk p ​ ( n 2 ) p\binom{n}{2} . Randomized quicksort with noisy comparisons chooses a pivot q q uniformly at random from the current list and compares it with every other key of the list, reading the answer on each such pair. It sends each key to the left or to the right sublist according to the answer, sorts the two sublists recursively, and outputs the left sublist, the pivot and the right sublist, in this order. We write H n = ∑ k = 1 n 1 / k H_{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}1/k for the n n -th harmonic number. Alonso et al. (2004) established 𝔼 ​ I ​ ( n , p ) ∼ n 2 ​ p \mathbb{E}I(n,p)\sim n^{2}p for quicksort with independent comparison errors in the regime n → ∞ n\to\infty , p → 0 p\to 0 and n ​ p → ∞ np\to\infty (their Theorem 2.2 and Remark 2.8). With comparisons wrong independently with probability p p , the expected number of inversions of randomized quicksort is p ⁡ ( n 2 + 3 ​ n − 2 ​ ( n + 1 ) ​ H n ) + O ⁡ ( p 2 ) p\,(n^{2}+3n-2(n+1)H_{n})+O(p^{2}) , where H n H_{n} is the n n -th harmonic number; the amplification tends to 2. Proof of Proposition 24 . We first identify randomized quicksort as a greedy decoder with an adaptive, pivot-first order. We then show that a single wrong comparison of key i i with pivot q q costs | i − q | |i-q| inversions. Weighting these costs by their comparison probabilities gives R QS ( p ) = p ( n 2 + 3 n − 2 ( n + 1 ) H n ) + O ( p 2 ) , n 2 + 3 ​ n − 2 ​ ( n + 1 ) ​ H n ( n 2 ) ⟶ 2 ( n → ∞ ) , R_{\mathrm{QS}}(p)=p\,\big(n^{2}+3n-2(n+1)H_{n}\big)+O(p^{2}),\qquad\frac{n^{2}+3n-2(n+1)H_{n}}{\binom{n}{2}}\longrightarrow 2\quad(n\to\infty), so that the amplification over the raw decoder tends to 2. Quicksort as a greedy decoder. The accepted answers compare each chosen pivot with the keys in its current sublist. They arrange the keys into a sequence of current sublists separated by pivots. Every total order that keeps this left-to-right arrangement, and orders each current sublist arbitrarily, is consistent with all answers read so far. Hence the relation between two keys of the same current sublist is not implied, and quicksort queries such a pair if one of the two keys becomes the pivot while both are still in that sublist. After a pivot q q has been compared with every key of its sublist, every pair ( l , r ) (l,r) with l l and r r on opposite sides of q q is implied by transitivity through q q , and it is skipped. More generally, a pair that quicksort never compares is split by some pivot that was compared with both of its keys, so its relation is implied by transitivity. Pairs inside a sublist are processed later, in the recursion. So quicksort accepts the non-implied pairs and skips the implied ones, in an adaptive order: first the pivot against the keys of its sublist, then the pairs across the two new sublists, then recursively inside each sublist. This is the greedy decoder with an adaptive pivot-first order, and its output is the unique total order consistent with all accepted answers. Pivots are selected by i.i.d. uniform priorities on the keys (the pivot of a sublist is its key of smallest priority), which are independent of the answers; the output is a function of the answers and the priorities, and with correct answers quicksort returns the true order. So Lemma 1 applies. Damage of a single wrong comparison. sections.text: We use HPI’s 1,879-record Cora file and duplicate-pair list ( Hasso Plattner Institute, n.d. ) . Duplicate-pair connected components define 182 entities, one per paper. Records use “field: value” pairs in the fixed order authors, title, journal, booktitle, institution, publisher, volume, pages, date and year. Qwen2.5-1.5B (base) ( Qwen Team, 2024 ) receives six hand-written citation-pair examples (three Yes, three No; none from Cora), then the test pair with the smaller record identifier first. It answers “same” when logit ⁡ ( Yes ) > logit ⁡ ( No ) \mathrm{logit}(\texttt{ Yes})>\mathrm{logit}(\texttt{ No}) . These next-token scores are used without sampling or fine-tuning. Similarity-first uses cosine similarity of normalized CLS embeddings from bge-small-en-v1.5 ( Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence, 2023 ) .

sections.heading: Experimental settings.
sections.text: The one-entity experiment uses the 23 entities with at least 20 records: 1,266 records, sizes 21 to 238, and all 62,423 within-entity pairs. For the multi-entity experiment, we group these entities into six blocks of three or four with nearby embedding centroids, mimicking similarity blocking. This includes comparisons between records from similar but distinct entities. Each entity contributes at most 30 records; blocks contain 87 to 120 records and 36,151 pairs in total. Pivot uses the multi-entity pipeline of Proposition 14 . All query orders reuse the same saved model answers. Primary pivot and random comparisons average over 200 orders per instance. The natural/shuffled error-placement control uses 30 matched order draws. Shuffled errors are uniformly redistributed within each entity. Similarity-first randomly breaks cosine ties: once per entity in the primary comparison and 200 times per multi-entity block. Amplification divides final wrong-pair counts by wrong answers across all candidate pairs, including skipped pairs. The 95% bootstrap intervals resample entities (or blocks) with model answers fixed.

Error Propagation in Constraint Pruning with Noisy LLM Oracles Zhengtao Gui Weining Shen University of California, Irvine Abstract Constraint pruning saves queries to a large language model (LLM) or another noisy oracle by skipping each yes/no question implied by answers accepted earlier, for example through transitivity. Entity-resolution systems and LLM-based rankers use this idea. However, their analyses typically assume a correct oracle. We argue that pruning should be judged by its risk when the oracle errs, since an accepted wrong answer spreads to every question it implies. When each answer is wrong independently with small probability ε \varepsilon , the first-order risk is set by how many facts one wrong answer corrupts on average. We consider two kinds of constraints. For implication rules, as in taxonomies, pruning in a random order adds no first-order risk: a wrong answer that would change k k facts is accepted with probability 1 / k 1/k , so it costs one fact on average. Rules with s s premises break this balance: a wrong answer at a premise shared by r r rules can cost order r 1 − 1 / s r^{1-1/s} facts. For entity resolution with m m records of one entity, the first-order risk equals ε \varepsilon times the Wiener index (the total pairwise distance) of the spanning tree built by the query order. Pivot orders, which first compare one record with all others, amplify errors by less than 2 and are optimal; random orders by order m 1 / 3 m^{1/3} ; the common most-similar-first order is the worst in one dimension and, for large m m , worse than random in two. With several entities, the cost of wrongly merging two does not depend on how many others exist. Simulations agree with every predicted constant within sampling error. 1 INTRODUCTION Constraint pruning reduces the cost of collecting related yes/no facts from an oracle, such as an LLM or a human annotator, whose answers may be wrong. In entity resolution, a system asks whether two records refer to the same entity and skips pairs implied by transitivity ( Wang et al., 2013 ; Vesdapunt et al., 2014 ) . For example, accepting that A A and B B are the same and that B B and C C are the same determines the answer for A A and C C without another query. Similar propagation occurs when enforcing entailment and contradiction constraints between LLM beliefs ( Mitchell et al., 2022 ) , skipping comparisons in LLM ranking ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ) , or propagating orientation hints in causal discovery ( Meek, 1995 ; Long et al., 2023 ; Lyu et al., 2026 ) . However, an accepted error can also propagate to unqueried facts. If A A , B B and C C belong to one entity, a correct “same” answer for A , B A,B followed by a wrong “different” answer for B , C B,C implies a wrong “different” answer for A , C A,C . In the synthetic citation records of Figure 1 , one oracle error thus produces two final wrong decisions and saves one query, and the output is still logically consistent. Query counts alone cannot capture this cost. Prior work studies recovery probabilities, assumes deterministic oracles or examines the robustness of query structures ( Long et al., 2023 ; Hiremath et al., 2026 ; Agrawal et al., 2026 ; Galhotra et al., 2018 ) . Figure 1: Propagation in three synthetic citation records of one publication: one wrong answer produces two wrong pair decisions and saves one query. We study greedy closure decoding : process questions in an order, skip those implied by accepted answers, and otherwise query and accept the oracle’s answer, without revisiting earlier decisions. We measure risk by the expected number of final wrong facts, including inferred ones. The raw baseline asks every question and uses its answer unchanged, without enforcing consistency. Both procedures use the same potential answers: the answers the oracle would give if each question were asked. In single-error analysis , we make one potential answer wrong and keep all others correct. We count the final wrong facts caused by each error location, averaging over query orders when they are random. In Figure 1 , damage is 2; it is 0 if earlier correct answers imply and skip the wrong question. Under independent errors of small probability ε \varepsilon ( Long et al., 2023 ; Hiremath et al., 2026 ) , events with two or more errors have probability O ⁡ ( ε 2 ) O(\varepsilon^{2}) for a fixed finite instance. A reduction lemma expresses risk as ε \varepsilon times the sum of single-error damages, plus O ⁡ ( ε 2 ) O(\varepsilon^{2}) . The term linear in ε \varepsilon is the first-order risk ; its ratio to the raw baseline’s n ​ ε n\varepsilon is the error amplification , where n n counts questions. Random-order ranking and Meek propagation are not analyzed. Using single-error analysis, we derive the following first-order risk laws: • Risk conservation for pairwise constraints. For every satisfiable 2-CNF theory, including implications and pairwise contradictions, uniformly random orders give mean single-error damage 1 for unfixed facts and 0 for facts fixed by the constraints. Pruning therefore does not increase first-order risk over raw decoding ( Section 4 ). • Error amplification through a shared premise. For k k Horn rules with s ≥ 2 s\geq 2 premises each and one shared false premise, we derive the exact mean damage of a single wrong answer there, growing as Θ ⁡ ( k 1 − 1 / s ) \Theta(k^{1-1/s}) under uniformly random orders, for fixed s s ( Theorem 6 ). • Relating query order to tree structure. For m m records of one entity, independent errors at a common rate give first-order risk equal to that rate times the noiseless query tree’s Wiener index (total pairwise tree distance). Pivot stars minimize this risk among greedy orders, with amplification below 2; random orders give Θ ⁡ ( m 1 / 3 ) \Theta(m^{1/3}) , and similarity-first can be worse under Theorem 11 ’s embedding assumptions. We also give bounds for multiple errors at any error rate ( Section 5.1 ). • Locality of a single false merge. With only one wrong answer, false-merge damage depends only on the two affected entities. This yields separate within-entity and cross-entity first-order risks. We give bounds, exact small cases and the pivot pipeline’s exact first-order formula; the large-cluster growth exponent remains a conjecture ( Section 5.2 ). We test the theoretical predictions and compare query orders using simulations and LLM answers on the Cora citation data ( Section 6 ). 2 RELATED WORK Noisy recovery and tree structure. Work on probabilistic unclean databases relates integrity constraints to minimum-repair and maximum-likelihood decoding ( De Sa et al., 2019 ; Gilad et al., 2023 ) . Other studies consider noisy graph-label recovery ( Globerson et al., 2015 ; Foster et al., 2018 ; Heidari et al., 2020 ; Lee et al., 2022 ; Jin et al., 2026 ) , correlation clustering ( Makarychev et al., 2015 ) , same-cluster queries ( Mazumdar and Saha, 2017b ) and noisy sorting ( Feige et al., 1994 ; Braverman and Mossel, 2008 ) . Their main goals are query efficiency or global recovery guarantees, usually at constant noise ( Banerjee and Shen, 2022 ) . Our tree-based analysis uses Kruskal’s construction ( Kruskal, 1956 ) , extremal properties of the Wiener index ( Dobrynin et al., 2001 ) , and results on random and spatial spanning trees ( Addario-Berry et al., 2009 ; Addario-Berry et al., 2017 ; Aizenman et al., 1999 ) . Entity resolution and LLM comparisons. Crowdsourced entity resolution uses transitivity ( Wang et al., 2013 ; Vesdapunt et al., 2014 ) . Analyses of query ordering typically assume a correct oracle ( Firmani et al., 2016 ; Mazumdar and Saha, 2017a ) ; robust methods add verification queries ( Galhotra et al., 2018 ) or weaken transitivity ( Gruenheid et al., 2015 ) . Recent LLM work studies prompt sensitivity ( Gui et al., 2026 ) and matching errors ( Peeters et al., 2025 ) , compares matching strategies ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , filters candidates using matching feedback ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , and balances quality and cost through operator and model selection ( Guo et al., 2026 ) . Ranking work addresses non-transitive preferences and baseline-sensitive rankings ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , presentation-order and transitivity inconsistencies ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) , and risks from long inference chains ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ) . These studies improve matching, ranking or query allocation. We analyze how an accepted wrong answer causes errors in inferred decisions. Logical consistency and causal hints. Belief-correction methods enforce entailment and contradiction relations ( Mitchell et al., 2022 ) . Logic.py translates natural-language puzzles into formal problems for a constraint solver ( Kesseli et al., 2025 ) . Causal discovery methods elicit and propagate hints about edge orientations ( Long et al., 2023 ; Lyu et al., 2026 ; Kıcıman et al., 2024 ) , while Guess2Graph uses unreliable expert guesses to order conditional-independence tests ( Hiremath et al., 2026 ) . These methods correct answers or select hints. We study a sequential decoding process that accepts oracle answers in order and keeps accepted answers fixed during subsequent inference. 3 SETTING AND REDUCTION LEMMA Questions, constraints and noisy answers. There are n n binary questions. Complete vectors satisfying the constraints form the code 𝒞 ⊆ { 0 , 1 } n \mathcal{C}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n} ; each is a feasible codeword . They are the models (satisfying assignments) of a propositional theory Φ \Phi . The decoder knows the constraints but not the fixed truth x ⋆ ∈ 𝒞 x^{\star}\in\mathcal{C} . We study implication, 2-CNF and definite Horn theories ( Section 4 ), partitions under “same entity” transitivity ( Section 5 ), and total orders under “before” transitivity ( Section A.4 ). The oracle’s potential answer y i y_{i} to question i i is observed only if queried. Thus y = x ⋆ ⊕ Z y=x^{\star}\oplus Z , where Z i Z_{i} are independent Bern ⁡ ( ε ) \mathrm{Bern}(\varepsilon) variables: Z i = 1 Z_{i}=1 flips the true answer and Z i = 0 Z_{i}=0 leaves it unchanged. Under uniformly random query orders, 2-CNF constraints do not increase first-order risk over raw answers, while shared-premise Horn rules can amplify errors. In record matching, one-entity first-order risk is determined by pairwise distances on the noiseless query tree. Under independent, equal-rate errors, pivot minimizes this risk among greedy orders. With one wrong answer, false merges affect only two entities. Simulations support the formulas and show pivot’s advantage over random order at the tested higher error rates. The Cora results show that tree shape and error locations both matter: uniformly redistributing errors removes similarity-first’s advantage over pivot.
